Full text

Abstract

Empathy supports effective caregiving, as parents rely on infants' non-verbal signals to guide their responses. Emerging evidence suggests that men undergo hormonal and neural changes related to empathy during the transition to parenthood. This study investigated men's empathic reactions towards children by comparing groups at different stages of fatherhood to test a proposal that expecting and first-time fathers show heightened empathic reactivity to children's distress. With pre-registered analyses, we compared three groups: expecting fathers (N = 35), first-time fathers (N = 44), and fathers of more than one child (N = 39). Participants completed a Picture task and a Video task involving emotional child stimuli. Their facial muscle responses were measured using facial electromyography (zygomaticus and corrugator muscles).

Participants also reported their subjective emotional reactions and provided saliva samples for testosterone assessment. Only in the Picture task first-time fathers showed stronger corrugator activity to negative child stimuli when compared with expecting fathers, while self-reported empathy did not differentiate the groups. Testosterone was negatively associated with corrugator responses toward negative pictures of children, but only among expecting fathers.

Although group differences were modest, these findings point to subtle shifts in fathers' responsiveness during the transition to parenthood and indicate that early fatherhood may represent a period of heightened responsiveness to child distress.

Introduction

Affective empathy, the automatic emotional resonance with another's emotional state (De Waal & Preston, 2017; Singer, & Lamm, 2009), is a crucial element of parenting as it allows parents to simulate their child's emotional experience. Children's emotional signals shape parent-child interaction and proximity by motivating empathic reactions to the child's cues (Bell & Ainsworth, 1972; George & Solomon, 2008). Consequently, affective empathy supports parents in recognizing and addressing their preverbal infant's needs, mobilizing protective action in times of threat, and fostering the appropriate, contingent responsiveness that underlies sensitive caregiving (Ainsworth et al., 1978; Bos, Spencer, & Buisman, 2026).

Given that affective empathy operates through rapid, automatic emotional resonance, it is reflected in measurable physiological responses to children's affective signals.

Affective stimuli such as facial expressions or scenes depicting emotionally positive or negative situations elicit rapid, automatic changes in facial muscle activity that are associated with changes in affective states (Kraaijenvanger et al., 2017) and empathic reactions (Braadbaart et al., 2014). Such facial responses to affective stimuli can be measured with facial electromyography (EMG; Cacioppo et al., 1986; Dimberg et al., 2000). Negative affective stimuli typically produce corrugator supercilii (COR) activity in the brow region, associated with frowning and negative affect, while positive affective stimuli elicit zygomaticus major (ZYG) activity in the cheek muscle region, related to smiling and positive affect (Larsen, Norris, & Cacioppo, 2003; Tan et al., 2012). Because these facial muscle responses can reflect rapid, automatic affective reactions to others' emotional expressions, facial EMG has been used as an index of affective responding in research on empathy.

Muscle reactions are fast and automatic: they occur as a response to emotional stimuli even when they are subconscious (Dimberg, Thunberg, & Elmehed, 2000) and when there is attempt to inhibit facial muscle activation (Korb, Grandjean, & Scherer, 2010).

Importantly, research has indicated that individuals with higher levels of self-reported empathy exhibit greater facial muscle activity when observing others' emotions (Dimberg et al., 2011; Dimberg & Thunberg, 2012; Van der Graaff et al., 2016). These studies assessed empathy using self-report measures, although the specific measures and dimensions of empathy differed across studies. Moreover, the studies examined responses to both positive and negative emotional stimuli, including happy and angry facial expressions (Dimberg et al., 2011; Dimberg & Thunberg, 2012) and happy and sad emotional stimuli (Van der Graaff et al., 2016).

In the present study we investigated men's facial muscle activation as a marker of affective empathy and emotional reactivity towards children. We investigated whether men's facial muscle responses to images of children's emotional signals and situations indicating danger to the child are modulated by men's parental status. In a cross-sectional design we compared fathers at different points of transition to fatherhood: expecting men (expecting first child), first-time fathers (fathers who had one infant), and experienced fathers (fathers with two or more children).

The transition to fatherhood

Becoming a father for the first time is a period marked by significant neural and hormonal changes that are associated with responsiveness to child signals in new fathers (Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2019; Kuo et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018). Fathers' physiological changes can begin already during their partner's pregnancy (Diaz-Rojas et al., 2021) and become more pronounced after the child is born (Diaz-Rojas et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2014).

For example, a number of studies have found that men's testosterone declines as they become a father (Gettler, McDade, Feranil, and Kuzawa, 2011; Gray et al., 2002; Meijer et al., 2019; Saxbe et al., 2017), a change that is hypothesized to help the new father to increase their focus on their family and childcare, instead of competition and mating (Archer, 2006; Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2022; Gettler, McDade, Feranil, & Kuzawa, 2011 ). Fleming et al. (2002) proposed that, besides shifting men's focus towards parenting, the drop in testosterone during the transition to fatherhood may be associated with changes in responses to infant distress. They found that, compared with childless men, fathers responded to infant distress with greater self-reported sympathy and urge to help the infant, and that these responses were stronger among fathers with lower testosterone levels (Fleming et al., 2002). At the same time, testosterone may be involved in motivational processes relevant to parental protection. Recent theoretical work proposes that caregiving encompasses both nurturant and protective responses, with empathic processes potentially contributing to the motivation to engage in both forms of caregiving (Bos et al., 2026). Consistent with this framework, preliminary results showed that, in women, testosterone administration increased facial EMG reactivity to images of children designed to elicit empathic responses, with the increase appearing strongest in women with higher self-reported protective care motivation (Bos et al., 2021). Together, these findings suggest that testosterone-related changes may influence both sensitivity to others' emotional states and the mobilization of protective action, processes that are central to parental responses to infant threat ( Van 't Veer et al., 2019).

However, the specific effects of testosterone on fathers' empathic responses to children have yet to be studied comprehensively.

New and experienced fathers

The period of expecting and caring for a pre-verbal infant for the first time might represent a phase during which a parent's responsiveness to child signals is particularly heightened (Gettler et al., 2021; Li et al., 2018; Storey et al., 2000). Evidence from mothers suggests that neural responses to infant affective cues are modulated by parity (Maupin et al., 2019; Vuoriainen et al., 2022). Compared to multiparous mothers, primiparous mothers showed heightened attention-related neural responses towards infant cues (Bunderson et al., 2020; Maupin et al., 2016) and rated them as higher in subjective emotional arousal (Parsons et al., 2021). Longitudinal evidence further indicates that mothers' early attentional bias toward infant distress diminishes across their child's first year (Hiraoka et al., 2023). Enhanced reactivity in first-time parents may serve an adaptive function, focusing attention on infant cues and facilitating the acquisition of parenting skills. Moreover, biological changes associated with the transition to parenthood may be more pronounced with the first child, potentially resulting in reduced reactivity when caring for subsequent children. However, it remains unknown whether these hypothesized parity effects characterize fathers as findings from mothers cannot be assumed to directly generalize to fathers.

Although it has now been documented that men undergo physiological changes during transition to parenthood, studies on how fathers' experience as a parent (operationalized as the child's age or the number of children) might modulate their responses to infant emotional cues are currently lacking. Our previous study (Veistola et al., 2025) addressed this question by comparing childless men, expecting men, and fathers on affective empathy. In a large online sample, we showed the participants images of children in naturalistic, emotional contexts (Spencer et al., 2022) and they self-reported their affective empathy towards the child. An unexpected exploratory finding that fathers with multiple children reported lower empathy compared to expecting and first-time fathers prompted us to examine fathers with different amounts of childcare experience more closely in a separate sample. Overall, in our two samples, we found that fathers expecting a child or living with a young infant showed heightened self-reported affective empathy towards children's emotional cues, as compared to childless men and fathers with older children irrespective of parity (Veistola et al., 2025). The previous study provided us with initial evidence that the amount of childcare experience a man has might also affect their empathic responses to child cues.

Some evidence suggests that fathers' physiology may differ between first-time and more experienced fathers. After an initial postnatal decline in testosterone, fathers may show a testosterone rebound as their child grows (Corpuz et al., 2021; Rosenbaum et al., 2018).

Testosterone decline may be prolonged in fathers who cohabit with their children (Mascaro et al., 2014), although it remains unclear whether cohabitation itself suppresses the rebound (Gettler et al., 2015). Parenting experience can also influence fathers' immediate physiological reactions to child signals (Fleming et al., 2002; Gettler et al., 2021). For instance, first-time fathers were found to show an increase in oxytocin when holding their first-born, while fathers with multiple children showed no change in oxytocin levels between pre-and post-holding (Gettler et al., 2021). Importantly, such physiological responses are likely shaped not only by parity but also by the level of involvement and the type of caregiving behavior fathers provide.

Yet, despite initial insights into fathers' physiological changes, direct evidence connecting fathers' childcare experience to empathy-related physiological responses toward children remains scarce. Investigating how parenting experience shapes fathers' physiological responses is essential for advancing a balanced understanding of human caregiving, especially as fathers' involvement and their influence on child development become increasingly recognized (Bakermans-Kranenburg et al., 2019).

Present study

Building on prior findings that fathers' empathic and physiological responses to child signals may vary with parenting experience, the present study directly examines fathers' physiological reactions to children's emotional cues and threat-related situations. Specifically, we assessed fathers' empathic responding by measuring facial muscle activation as they viewed children's emotional expressions and scenarios involving potential danger. Participants completed two tasks measuring affective empathy during an EMG recording. First, we presented fathers with images of children in naturalistic situations that had either negative, positive, or neutral emotional valence (Picture task; Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022).

Second, participants watched videos of lifelike scenarios in which a realistic infant doll was in a threatening or neutral situation (Video task; Lotz et al., 2021; Van 't Veer et al., 2019). We compared three distinct father groups: expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers. Expecting fathers were fathers whose partner was expecting their first child, first-time fathers had their first infant and no older children, and experienced fathers were fathers of an infant and one or more older children. Our main pre-registered research question examined whether expecting, first-time, and experienced fathers differ in their rapid facial muscle responses to children's emotional signals (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2W3SE).

Zygomaticus responses to positive pictures. We hypothesized, based on our previous findings (Veistola et al., 2025), that in the Picture task, responding to pictures of children in positive situations, expecting and first-time fathers would exhibit greater activation of the zygomaticus muscle compared to experienced fathers (H1a, one-sided). Additionally, we investigated whether expecting and first-time fathers differed in zygomaticus muscle activation in response to these positive images (H1b, two-sided).

Corrugator responses to negative pictures. We hypothesized that expecting and first-time fathers would show greater activation of the corrugator muscle than experienced fathers when viewing pictures of children in negative situations (H2a, one-sided). Again, we also investigated whether expecting and first-time fathers differed in corrugator muscle activation in these negative situations (H2b, two-sided).

Corrugator responses to infant-danger videos. Regarding the Video task, we hypothesized that expecting and first-time fathers would demonstrate greater corrugator muscle activation compared to experienced fathers when watching a video of an infant in danger (H3a, one-sided). We also assessed whether expecting and first-time fathers differed in their corrugator muscle activation in response to the videos depicting danger to the infant (H3b, twosided).

Secondary analyses.

In addition to the pre-registered hypotheses, we conducted several secondary and exploratory analyses. First, we examined whether salivary testosterone levels were associated with facial EMG responses to emotional child stimuli. Specifically, we assessed Spearman's rank-order correlations between testosterone levels and corrugator activity in response to negative pictures and zygomaticus activity in response to positive pictures, both across the full sample and within each participant group. This analysis was preregistered as a secondary analysis.

We also examined associations between facial EMG responses and individual differences in trait empathy (Interpersonal Reactivity Index; IRI), parental care and tenderness (PCAT), and paternal involvement with infants (PIWIS). These questionnaire-EMG correlations were pre-registered as secondary analyses. In addition, in exploratory analyses that were not pre-registered, we examined associations with depressive symptoms assessed using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS).

Finally, because the pre-registered analyses of the Video task did not reveal the expected effects of condition, we conducted additional post hoc analyses to examine whether responses might have been temporally localized within specific periods of the videos. These analyses were not pre-registered and were conducted for descriptive and hypothesis-generating purposes.

Methods

Participants and design

The current study was part of the TransParent project investigating responses to children's emotion cues during the transition to parenthood (Sinisalo et al., 2022 (Sinisalo et al., , 2025 (Sinisalo et al., , 2026;; Veistola et al., 2025; Vuoriainen et al., 2022 Vuoriainen et al., , 2026)). We ran a cross-sectional laboratory study (N = 118) with three independent groups: expecting men (N = 35), first-time fathers (N = 44), and experienced fathers (N = 39). Descriptive statistics are reported in Table 1. We determined the total sample size with a power analysis ('pwr' package; Champely, 2020) to be 100 to reliably detect a small to medium effect size in a general linear model at alpha level 0.05 with statistical power of .80. We collected the data between June 2022 and April 2023. The study was performed according to the Declaration of Helsinki and the study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Tampere Region.

Expecting participants were primarily recruited through the maternity clinics of the City of Tampere. Nurses informed fathers about the study during prenatal visits either directly or their pregnant partners were asked to relay the information to the child's father. The parent received a brief study brochure from the nurse. Additionally, we distributed study advertisements to the maternity clinics, and the study was advertised through social media.

Fathers of young infants were recruited using contact information of parents of infants born in Tampere and surrounding areas obtained from the Finnish Digital and Population Data Services Agency. We sent parents a research brochure by mail or email. In the research brochure, we requested men interested in study participation to provide their contact information (name, email, and phone number) either directly to the researchers or through a registration form on the project's website. Upon receiving the contact information, we contacted potential participants by phone to provide further information about the study, ensured that inclusion criteria were met, and arranged the timing of the first research visit.

We included participants who were at least 18 years old, fluent in Finnish, and cohabiting with their child's mother. Expecting men's pregnant partner was expecting their first child in their third trimester. Fathers were required to have an approximately 4-month-old infant. The fathers were further divided into two groups: those with no older children (firsttime fathers) and those with older children (experienced fathers) in addition to the infant. We excluded participants if they had a diagnosis for a psychiatric or neurological condition, if their infant was born premature or had a congenital disease, or if the participant was using anabolic steroids, given their impact on testosterone levels.

Procedure and Measures

We presented the tasks to the participants using E-Prime 2.0 (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA) and participants completed all tasks on a computer in a laboratory setting. Self-report measures were sent to the participant after the visit, and they completed them online on their own time.

Picture task

To assess participants' facial and self-reported emotional responses to children's positive and negative emotions, we used a task previously developed and employed by Bos and colleagues (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022). The task uses grayscale images of children in naturalistic situations and has previously been used to investigate empathic responses towards children, combining facial electromyographic responses with self-reported ratings of compassion and positive affect (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022; Veistola et al., 2025).

The images depicted children in negative (e.g., a child crying alone on the street), positive (e.g., a child playing with a parent), or neutral (e.g., a child sitting at a dining table) situations. There were 10 images of each valence, that were presented for two seconds in a random order. Each image was preceded by a fixation cross (1 s). In total, the participants viewed 30 images.

The images were each followed by two questions (self-paced), resulting in 60 self-report responses. Participants gave their answers on a continuous numerical scale (range 1-9) by clicking a number on the screen after each picture. The first question measured positive affect: "How positive do you feel about the picture?" (1 = not at all positive,9 = very positive).

The second question measured compassion: "How much compassion do you feel for the child?"

(1 = not at all,9 = very much). There was no time limit for the response, and response latency was recorded but not included as a covariate because the self-report responses occurred after the predefined EMG measurement windows. We did not form hypotheses regarding the response latency.

Video task

To assess participants' facial empathic reactions towards threat to an infant, in the second task participants viewed threatening and neutral videos. We used a video task that has previously been used to investigate responses to infants in threatening versus neutral situations in the context of paternal protection, including with neuroimaging and hormonal measures (Lotz et al., 2021; van 't Veer et al., 2019). However, it has not previously been used or validated for assessing facial electromyographic responses. In the task, participants watched 12 videos of scenarios in which a lifelike infant doll was in a threatening situation (e.g., in a pram that slides into a canal) and 12 matched neutral videos in which the context was identical but there was no threat to the infant doll (e.g., in a pram that is safely parked next to a canal).

Each video lasted 6 seconds and was repeated twice resulting in 24 threat and 24 control trials.

The trials were separated into two blocks containing only threat or control videos. We used a blocked instead of a randomized presentation because frequency-based EEG and heart rate measures were also collected during the task (not reported here). Each video was preceded by a fixation cross (1 s). The blocks were presented in the same order for all participants, with the threat video block presented first, followed by the control video block. Within the video blocks, the individual videos were presented in random order.

EMG data acquisition and analysis

We placed two pairs of Ag/AgCl electrodes on the left side of the participant's face, following established guidelines for facial EMG recording (Fridlund & Cacioppo, 1986).

One pair was attached over the corrugator supercilii muscle (COR; next to the eyebrow) and the other pair over the zygomaticus major muscle (ZYG; on the cheek between the ear and corner of the mouth) for muscle activation (EMG) measurement. Each pair's electrodes were placed 1 cm apart from each other. A ground electrode was attached on top of the participant's seventh cervical vertebra (C7). Before attaching the electrodes, the skin was gently rubbed with disinfectant, and the electrodes were filled with conductive electrolyte gel (Signa gel).

EMG signals were sampled at 1000 Hz using an actiCHamp Plus (Brain Products GmbH) amplifier. Offline, we pre-processed the data with BrainVision Analyzer 2.2. and R Statistical Software (v 4.4.1, R Core Team, 2024), following recommendations for EMG signal acquisition and processing (Fridlund & Cacioppo, 1986; Rutkowska et al., 2024). The raw data were first band-pass filtered at 28-499 Hz with a notch filter of 50 Hz and then rectified. For the Picture task, we segmented data for each 2 s trial into 250-ms time bins time-locked to stimulus onset, resulting in 8 time bins. For the Video task, we segmented the data for each 6 s trial into 500-ms time bins time-locked to stimulus onset, resulting in 12 time bins. For both tasks, we used a 1 s baseline preceding each stimulus. One participant from the expectant fathers' group was removed due to missing data resulting from a technical error during the EMG data recording during the Video task. Thus, the Video task analyses were done with 117 participants.

For every participant, muscle, and time bin, we calculated that participant's average EMG activation and its standard deviation across all conditions. Each EMG value was then compared to the mean from its own participant-muscle-time-bin combination, and values more than three standard deviations above this reference were marked as artifacts. There is no single established criterion for artifact rejection in facial EMG, and different thresholds and procedures have been used in previous studies (Rutkowska et al., 2024). Visual inspection indicated that the data were relatively clean, and we therefore selected a threshold intended to limit the removal of plausible facial muscle activity while identifying prominent artifacts, such as eye blinks. With the aforementioned criterion, 1.38% of the data from the Picture task was detected as artifacts. The number of artifacts did not differ between the time bins, F(8) = 0.32, p = .959, nor between groups, F(2) = .51, p = .599. From the Video task, 1.37% of the data was detected as artifacts. The number of artifacts did not differ between the time bins, F(12) = 0.60, p = .846. The artifacts differed between groups, F(2) = 6.10, p = .002, however, the differences were very small in practice. Closer inspection showed that the experienced fathers' group had 0.17% more artifacts compared to first-time fathers, and 0.26% more artifacts compared to expecting fathers. We removed only the individual time bins flagged as artifacts, while retaining all other time bins within the same trial.

After removing time bins with artifacts, we standardized EMG activity for each participant, muscle, and time bin. We calculated a participant's mean and standard deviation of EMG activity across all conditions. We then converted each EMG value into a z-score using the mean and standard deviation from its own participant-muscle-time-bin combination. We performed baseline correction on these z-scored values by subtracting the z-scored activity in the 1000 ms pre-stimulus baseline window from the post-stimulus time bins. We used these standardized, baseline-corrected values as outcomes in the linear mixed-effects models.

Testosterone measurement and analysis

Participants' baseline testosterone was measured from saliva samples. The participants gave a saliva sample after receiving information about the study and signing a consent form, before any other measurements. To control for unwanted variation in testosterone levels, the participants were instructed to refrain from heavy exercise and drinking alcohol for 24 hours, eating or drinking for one hour, and smoking for two hours prior to the study visit.

The samples were collected with a Salivette® (Sarstedt, Nümbrecht, Germany) polypropylene swab. Participants chewed the swab for one minute and then inserted the swab into a polyethylene container without touching the swab with their hands or the container with their mouth. The swab was initially stored at -20 to -30°C before being transported in dry ice to a liquid nitrogen freezer (-80°C). Salivary testosterone was analyzed with enzyme immunoassay for the quantitative determination of free testosterone in saliva (EIA, IBL International, RE52631) in the Finnish Institute of Occupational Health (Helsinki, Finland). Assay performance characteristics are reported in the manufacturer's instructions for use (IBL International GmbH, 2025).

Statistical analyses

We examined task and group effects with pre-registered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NJ5ZA) linear mixed-effects analyses using the lmer and lm4 packages (Bates et al., 2015 , Kuznetsova et al., 2017) in R Statistical Software (v 4.4.1, R Core Team, 2024). We initially attempted to fit a multilevel model with the most complex structure allowed by our research design (Barr et al., 2013), which included random intercepts and slopes for all predictors. However, this model did not converge due to insufficient data support and computational limitations. Hence, we simplified the random structure until the model converged successfully. Our approach allowed us to retain the essential elements of our preregistered plan while ensuring model stability. We obtained p-values from significant omnibus F tests, using type III ANOVAs via Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom method (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

Before hypothesis testing, we examined whether the task worked as intended, i.e., whether the task conditions produced responses in expected direction reflected in facial EMG and evaluative responses. For the Picture task, we examined the effect of affective condition by including EMG data (COR and ZYG) and ratings (compassion and positive affect) into separate models with affective condition (negative vs. positive vs. neutral) as a fixed effect.

For EMG data analyses, we added time as a fixed factor in interaction with affective condition.

As random effects, we included intercepts for participants, as well as by-participant slopes for condition. This resulted in the following base model for the Picture task: EMG data / Ratings ~ 1 + Condition * Time + (1 + Condition | Participant).

For the Video task, we examined the effect of the threat video condition by including EMG data (for the COR) into a model with video condition (control vs. threat) as a fixed effect. Time was added as a fixed factor in interaction with video condition. As random effects, we included intercepts for participants, as well as by-participant slopes for condition.

This resulted in the following base model: EMG data ~ 1 + Condition * Time + (1 + Condition | Participant).

Next, we tested our hypotheses about Group effects on our outcomes for the Picture task. We entered Group into the models in interaction with the fixed effects of the base Because salivary testosterone was not normally distributed, we used Spearman's rank-order correlations rather than Pearson correlations. This decision was made after inspecting the distribution of the testosterone data. Spearman's correlation is a nonparametric measure based on the ranks of the data and more robust with non-normal data distributions (Bishara & Hittner, 2012).

Declaration of generative AI in the manuscript preparation process

During the preparation of this work the first author used Microsoft Copilot for language checking for the Supplemental Materials and to aid in writing helper functions for data preprocessing in R. After using the AI tool, the first author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for the content of the published article.

Results

Task Effects

Corrugator Activity in Response to Affective Condition

Picture task. There was a significant main effect of affective condition, F(2, 118) = 78.22, p < .001, yet no main effect of time, F(1, 27925) = 0.03, p = .87. There was an interaction effect between affective condition and time on corrugator activity, F(2, 27924) = 189.30, p < .001. Over time, corrugator activity was significantly greater in response to negative images compared to neutral images, b = 0.11, t(27924) = 8.12, p < .001, and significantly lower in response to positive images compared to neutral images, b = -0.15, t(27924) = -11.26, p < .001. Figure 1 shows corrugator EMG activity over time following stimulus onset, averaged across the 10 images within each affective condition and across groups, with standard errors of the mean. Video task.

There was no main effect of affective condition, F(1, 66781) = 2.42, p = .120, and the main effect of time was not significant F(1, 66779) = 3.64, p = .057. The interaction effect between time and condition was also not significant, F(1, 66779) = 0.18, p = .671. We concluded that the Video task did not produce the expected results of greater corrugator activity in response to the threat videos and, hence, we did not proceed to analyze group effects. The null results are presented and further explored in the Supplemental Material.

Zygomaticus Activity in Response to Affective Condition

Picture task. There was a significant main effect of affective condition, F(2, 118) = 20.91, p < .001, but not of time, F(1, 27349) = 1.34, p = .25 (Figure 2). There was a significant interaction effect between affective condition and time on zygomaticus activity, F(2, 27351) = 43.05, p < .001. Over time, zygomaticus activity was significantly greater in response to positive images compared to neutral images, b = 0.06, t(27351) = 5.43, p < .001, and significantly lower in response to negative images compared to neutral images, b = -0.04, t(27351) = -3.80, p < .001. Figure 2 shows zygomaticus EMG activity over time following stimulus onset, averaged across the 10 images within each affective condition and across groups, with standard errors of the mean.

Zygomaticus muscle response to emotional images of children.

Self-Reported Compassion in Response to Affective Condition

We next examined self-reported compassion as a measure of participants' emotional responses to the children depicted in the Picture task. There was a significant effect of affective condition on self-reported compassion across the father groups, F(2, 118) = 178.17, p < .001. Pictures depicting children's negative emotions produced significantly higher self-reports of compassion compared to the positive, b = -1.38, t(118) = -8.26, p < .001, and neutral pictures, b = -1.95, t(118) = -15.66, p < .001.

Self-reported Positive Affect in Response to Affective Condition

We also examined self-reported positive affect as a measure of participants' emotional responses to the children depicted in the Picture task. There was a significant effect of affective condition, F(2, 118) = 2409, p < .001. Pictures displaying positive emotions produced greater self-reported positive affect across the father groups compared to the negative, b = -5.59, t(118) = -68.35, p < .001, and neutral pictures, b = -1.74, t(118) = -29.87, p < .001.

Group Effects

Group Differences in Corrugator Activity

There was a significant main effect of affective condition, F(1, 118) = 26.10, p < .001, and a significant main effect of time, F(1, 18.513) = 106.05, p < .001. Group membership did not have a significant main effect, F(2, 118) = 1.27, p = .28. We also found a significant interaction between condition and time, F(1, 18.513) = 66.61, p < .001. The condition × group and time × group interactions were not significant, Fs < 1.27, ps > .47. The three-way interaction between condition, time, and group was marginal, F(2, 18.513) = 2.93, p = .053. We compared the father groups according to our pre-registration, even though the interaction was not significant.

Corrugator activity increased significantly over time in response to negative images compared to neutral images, b = 0.15, t(18,513) = 6.99, p < .001. The increase was significantly larger for first-time fathers compared to expecting fathers, b = 0.07, t(18.513) = 2.30, p = .021 (Figure 3). The difference between experienced fathers and first-time fathers did not reach significance, b = -0.05, t(18.513) = -1.72, p = .086. Experienced and expecting fathers did not differ, b = 0.02, t(18.513) = 0.61, p = .543. Figure 3 shows corrugator EMG activity over time following stimulus onset for the three father groups and the three affective conditions, with standard errors of the mean. Group Differences in Zygomaticus Activity

There was a significant main effect of affective condition, F(1, 118) = 20.88, p < .001, and a significant main effect of time, F(1, 18.153) = 10.05, p = .002. Group membership did not have a significant main effect, F(2, 118) = 0.15, p = .860. We also found a significant interaction between condition and time, F(1, 18.154) = 26.10, p < .001. The condition × group and time × group interactions were not significant, Fs < 1.02, p > .360. The three-way interaction between condition, time, and group was also not significant, F(2, 18,154) = 2.00, p = .140.

Pre-registered follow-up tests showed that zygomaticus activity increased significantly over time in response to positive images compared to neutral images when group was in the model, b = 0.09, t(18,154) = 4.74, p < .001. The increase was marginally smaller for expecting fathers compared to first-time fathers, b = -0.06, t(18,154) = -1.94, p = .052. (Figure 4) The difference between experienced fathers and first-time fathers was not significant, b = -0.04, t(18,154) = -1.31, p = .190. Experienced and expecting fathers also did not differ from each other, b = 0.02, t(18,154) = 0.65, p = .517. Normalized EMG scores relative to baseline are plotted on the y-axis, with the horizontal

Group Differences in Self-reported Compassion

We next examined group differences in self-reported compassion as a measure of participants' emotional responses to the children depicted in the Picture task. There was a significant effect of condition when we added group to the model, F(1, 118) = 226.65, p < .001. Negatively valenced pictures produced significantly higher self-reports of compassion compared to the neutral pictures, b = 1.92, t = 8.39, p < .001. Group did not have a main effect, F(2, 118) = 1.21, p = .303, and the group × condition interaction effect was not significant, F(2, 118) = .20, p = .821.

Group Differences in Self-reported Positive Affect

We also examined group differences in self-reported positive affect as a measure of participants' emotional responses to the children depicted in the Picture task. There was a significant effect of condition when we added group to the model, F(1, 118) = 883.118, p < .001. Positively valenced pictures produced significantly higher self-reports of positive affect compared to the neutral pictures, b = 1.78, t = 17.38, p < .001. Group did not have a main effect, F(2, 118) = .34, p = .716, and the group × condition interaction effect was not significant, F(2, 118) = .633, p = .533.

Associations Between Testosterone and Facial EMG Responses

Across the full sample, in the Picture task, testosterone was not significantly correlated with corrugator responses toward negative images, r s = -0.11, p = .233, nor with zygomatic responses toward positive images, r s = -0.15, p = .100. Within the expecting fathers' group, testosterone was significantly negatively correlated with corrugator responses toward negative images, r s = -0.50, p = .002, indicating that higher testosterone levels were associated with reduced corrugator responses. The correlation between testosterone and zygomatic responses in this group was not significant, r s = -0.28, p = .108. In the first-time father group, we found no significant correlations between testosterone and either corrugator, r s = 0.06, p = .694, or zygomatic responses, r s = 0.05, p = .744. Similarly, in the experienced group, testosterone was not significantly associated with corrugator, r s = -0.01, p = .957, or zygomaticus responses, r s = -0.23, p = .166.

Discussion

Empathy plays an important role in caregiving and the moment-to-moment interactions between a caregiver and a non-verbal infant. The primary aim of this study was to examine whether paternal group membership (expecting, first-time and experienced fathers) is associated with facial EMG responses and self-reported empathy to affective child stimuli.

Overall, the hypothesized group differences were small but partly in line with our hypotheses.

We used a task that has been previously linked to EMG responses with robust condition effects (Spencer et al., 2022). As in previous studies, the affective condition produced the expected pattern of facial muscle responses, with positive child emotion displays producing greater zygomaticus responses and negative child emotions producing greater increase in corrugator activity across the three father groups (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022). The pre-registered planned comparisons showed that first-time fathers exhibited a greater corrugator response toward negative emotions in children than expecting fathers, whereas the difference between experienced and first-time fathers was marginal and did not reach the pre-set significance threshold. For zygomaticus responses, we could observe a similar pattern, although the grouprelated differences were marginal and did not reach our pre-set significance thresholds. Selfreported compassion and positive affect varied by affective condition in the expected directions, but did not differ by group, suggesting that paternal status did not influence subjective emotional and empathic experience strongly enough in this study.

Beyond facial EMG and self-reports, hormonal analyses showed that salivary testosterone levels were generally unrelated to facial muscle reactivity in the full sample.

However, within the expecting group, higher testosterone was associated with reduced corrugator responses to negative stimuli. At present, evidence on how testosterone relates to emotion-related facial muscle responses is limited, and findings from related measures are mixed. An experimental study in women reported increased affective facial responding following testosterone administration (Bos et al., 2021), whereas other work has linked higher administered or endogenous testosterone levels to lower empathic or affective responses to others' emotions (e.g., Hermans et al., 2006; Procyshyn et al., 2020), often in interaction with other hormones (Zilioli et al., 2015). These findings provide evidence for both positive and negative associations between testosterone and emotional responding, making strong directional predictions difficult. The prior experimental study was conducted in women and not in men transitioning to fatherhood, a period in which the role of testosterone remains debated (Meijer et al., 2019). In this context, our findings are not inconsistent with either direction of association reported previously, but they tentatively suggest that testosterone may be particularly relevant for emotional responding in expecting fathers. Lower testosterone in expecting fathers might be particularly helpful considering evidence that lower prenatal testosterone levels have been associated with greater partner-and child-directed investment in men (Rilling et al., 2025). The absence of correlations between testosterone and EMG responses in first-time and experienced fathers might also suggest that testosterone's role in transition to fatherhood may be temporary and subside over time (Corpuz, D'Alessandro, & Collom, 2021).

Notably, we did not observe differences in testosterone levels among the three father groups in our sample, even though previous longitudinal studies have documented decreases in testosterone across the transition to fatherhood (Gettler, McDade, Feranil, & Kuzawa, 2011). One possible explanation is that our study lacks a comparison group of childless men. Expectant fathers may have already experienced some reduction in testosterone, making them indistinguishable from the father groups. In addition, our sample is relatively small and cross-sectional, which limits statistical power compared with longitudinal designs.

Our sample size is particularly relevant for testosterone given that its documented decline tends to be modest in magnitude (Meijer et al., 2019).

Taken together, these results suggest that while emotional reactivity to affective stimuli was robust and follows well-established patterns (Bos et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2022), paternal group differences were subtle and primarily evident in physiological rather than selfreported measures. We interpret the greater corrugator responsivity as greater empathic reactivity to children's distress in first-time fathers. First-time parenthood is a developmental transition during which major changes in social roles and neurobiological functioning take place, supporting adjustment to the parental role (Feldman, 2015; Rilling & Mascaro, 2017; Saxbe et al., 2018). Our results showed enhanced facial responses specifically to children's negative emotions, which can function as salient signals of distress and need for caregiving.

Consistent with the interpretation of greater empathic reactivity in first-time fathers, a recent study reported greater corrugator responses to distressed faces in first-time mothers than nonmothers (Sinisalo et al., 2026). Enhanced reactivity to negative child signals at the early stages of transitioning to parenthood may therefore reflect increased sensitivity to children's signals that motivate protective or caregiving responses, ensuring that the child's needs are met and the caregiver's resources are allocated to the survival of the infant (Feldman, 2015; Rilling & Mascaro, 2017).

We found greater corrugator responses towards negative emotions specifically in first-time fathers compared to expecting fathers. We think this difference might emerge since, although expectant men begin to show subtle neurobiological changes during their partner's pregnancy (Diaz-Rojas, 2021), the neurobiological adjustments associated with the transition to parenthood tend to concentrate on the postnatal period for most fathers (Diaz-Rojas, 2023;

Bakermans-Kranenburg, 2019). Moreover, postnatal neurobiological changes in fathers depend on the amount of time spent on caregiving and the degree of exposure to their infant (Abrahams et al., 2014; Horstman et al., 2021). Therefore, the timing of neurobiological changes may help explain why postnatal fathers displayed heightened reactions to child signals compared to antenatal fathers, reflected here in their facial electromyographic responses.

Our results on the self-reported measures contrast those of Veistola et al. (2025) who found significant group differences in self-reported empathy at different stages of fatherhood. Namely, that study found that first-time fathers and expecting fathers reported more empathy (i.e., greater compassion) toward children in distressing situations using the same Picture task. However, the effect sizes were small, so not replicating these findings in our much smaller sample could be expected. The marginal and group-specific nature of the effects we found in the current study underscores the complexity of fatherhood-related changes and highlights the need for further research to clarify when and how these differences emerge.

It is not fully clear why the expected condition effects were not observed in the Video task, but several methodological features may have contributed. First, we presented the emotional and neutral videos in separate blocks with relatively short inter-stimulus intervals.

Although each trial included a 1000-ms pre-stimulus baseline, this interval may not have been sufficient for participants to return to an affectively neutral state after viewing emotionally intense clips, potentially leading to carryover effects. Second, unlike static images, the threatening content in the videos unfolded over time; in many clips, several seconds elapsed before the threatening event occurred. Because our EMG analyses were time-locked to video onset rather than to the exact moment when the threat occurred, early neutral segments may have diluted condition differences. Together, these features may have reduced the sensitivity of the Video task to detect condition-related EMG responses.

Limitations

A strength of this study is the multi-method approach combining EMG, hormonal measures, and self-reports, as well as precise control over the timing of fathers' participation at different stages of fatherhood. However, some limitations warrant caution. Although the Video task has been used previously in research on paternal protection and its neural and hormonal correlates (Lotz et al., 2021; van 't Veer et al., 2019), its ability to elicit facial electromyographic responses has not been established. Thus, the null EMG findings should be interpreted considering this limitation. Further, we did not have a group of childless men which means that we cannot compare the father groups to men who have not undergone the transition to fatherhood. This limits our ability to detect potential changes that may have already taken place among expecting men. Our sample was quite homogeneous in terms of socioeconomic background and generalizing these findings should be done with caution.

Conclusions

In the current study, first-time fathers exhibited greater corrugator responses to children's negative emotions compared to expecting fathers, and they also tended to show greater responses than experienced fathers. To better understand how these differences emerge, future research should consider including a comparison group of childless men in cross-sectional designs. Such a group would help clarify which changes are specifically linked to the transition into fatherhood. However, an even more informative next step would be longitudinal research beginning before pregnancy or the intention to become a parent.

Longitudinal designs are essential for identifying within-person changes across the transition to fatherhood and for distinguishing anticipatory processes from experience-driven changes. In addition, future work should incorporate measures of fathers' day-to-day caregiving involvement to better understand the role of caregiving experience in shaping changes in emotion-related facial muscle activity.
